definition: Deterrent means something that discourages an action by making its consequences feared; it works in advance, in the mind of whoever is weighing the act.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word deterrent. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know deterrent should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The dye packs cost the bank almost nothing, but their value as a deterrent has been priceless: three years now without a single robbery attempt.
A disincentive is milder than a deterrent: a fee or a hassle that quietly tilts the arithmetic of a choice, where a deterrent plants real fear of a consequence.
Prohibition goes further than a deterrent: a deterrent loads the choice with fear but leaves it open, while a prohibition removes the choice entirely and backs the ban with law.

A disincentive quietly tilts the arithmetic of a choice — a fee, a tax, a hassle that makes the act less rewarding. A deterrent works on the nerves instead: it threatens, and fear of the consequence does the discouraging even if the penalty is never once applied.

A curb is a check on something already underway — spending curbs rein in a budget that is moving. A deterrent gets there earlier: it discourages the act before it starts, in the mind of whoever is weighing it.

Deterrent means something that discourages an action by making its consequences feared; it works in advance, in the mind of whoever is weighing the act.
When the city hung bright-orange speed cameras over Millbrook Road, the council braced for an avalanche of fines.
It never came — barely two hundred tickets all year, against nine thousand projected.
Drivers spotted the cameras three blocks out and slowed; the deterrent was doing its work in windshields and rearview mirrors, and the punishments were hardly ever needed.

That gap between tickets projected and tickets written is the signature of a deterrent: it discourages the act in advance, by making the consequence feared, and it succeeds exactly to the degree that it never has to fire.
Had the city hidden the cameras and mailed nine thousand fines, it would have had punishment.
Visible and feared, it had prevention.

Deterrent belongs to arguments about crime, war, and rule-breaking: the posted fine, the visible camera, the arsenal maintained so that it never has to be used.
Keep it apart from an obstacle, which physically blocks, and a punishment, which arrives after the act — a deterrent does its work beforehand, in the imagination.
And spell with care: detergent only fights stains.

The mountain town of Weller's Gap could not afford a second traffic officer, so it bought a silhouette: a plywood cutout of a patrol car, positioned each week somewhere along the canyon road.
Drivers know about the decoy.
That, oddly, is why it works.

The cutout functions as a deterrent in the strict sense: it punishes no one and stops no one, but the flash of white and blue in the mirrors makes every driver ask whether this one is real — and ease off the gas before finding out.
Speeds in the canyon dropped eleven percent the first summer, though not a single ticket had been written there.
The town clerk keeps the receipts side by side: eighty dollars of plywood, she says, doing the advance work of fear.
